1 August 1998. Long-Term Capital Management, or LTCM, is a hedge fund: a private pool of investors' money that can trade almost anything. John Meriwether started it in February 1994. He was once vice chairman of the bond firm Salomon Brothers.

The fund finds two similar securities, such as bonds, whose prices have drifted slightly apart. Then it bets the gap will close. Each trade earns only a little, so the fund borrows heavily to make those gains bigger.

At the end of 1997, it gave some money back to investors but kept all its trades. Now it owes about 30 dollars for every dollar of its own money, which is called its capital.

Which would you check more carefully: the many small, likely gains or the rare, large loss?

That bank is made up: 4% to 5% is just an example to practise on. Real banks do change savings rates, though. A big reason is the central bank, the public body that steers a country's interest rates. When it raises its rate, banks usually pay more on savings too. In February 1994, the US central bank, called the Federal Reserve or "the Fed," is about to make that kind of decision. Its rate stands at 3%.

Partly. A credit card works the other way round: you pay the interest, not the bank. Some card rates follow the central bank's rate, but many barely move with it. The language is the same either way. Suppose your card's yearly rate rose by 1 percentage point. A trader would call that 100 bp, just like our savings rate going from 4% to 5%. The paise rule still works: 100 bp make 1 point, as 100 paise make ₹1.

It's because interest earns interest. That's called compounding. Put ₹100 in savings at 10% a year. In year 1 it earns ₹10, so you have ₹110. In year 2 the 10% is paid on ₹110, not ₹100. That year it earns ₹11, and you end with ₹121. Each year the pile is bigger, so the same rate adds more money. Over many years, that's why the growth seems to speed up later on.

CAGR stands for compound annual growth rate. It's the one steady yearly rate that would carry a start value to an end value, with interest earning interest along the way. Take our ₹100 that became ₹121 over 2 years. Its CAGR is 10%. Real investments jump around from year to year. CAGR flattens those jumps into one even yearly rate, so two investments are easy to compare. That's why your dad uses it.

Whether they gain or lose is what this Topic shows at its end.

Same answer as before, short version. Our bank is made up, so 4% to 5% is just for practice. In real life, banks often change savings rates after the central bank changes its own rate. **Points are the new rate minus the old rate.**

Do you find points by subtracting or by dividing?

Same reason as before: interest earns interest. Your ₹100 at 10% earns ₹10 in year 1. In year 2, the 10% is paid on ₹110, so it earns ₹11. Every year the pile is bigger. The same rate on a bigger pile adds more money. That's why growth looks slow at first and fast later on. This idea is called compounding.

CAGR means compound annual growth rate. It's the one even yearly rate that turns a starting amount into an ending amount, with interest earning interest. Our ₹100 grew to ₹121 over 2 years, so its CAGR is 10%. Real investments go up and down unevenly. CAGR smooths that into one steady yearly number, which makes two investments easy to compare.

August 1998, Greenwich, Connecticut. John Meriwether, once a top bond trader at Salomon Brothers, runs a fund called Long-Term Capital Management, or LTCM. It is a hedge fund: a private pool of rich investors' money that trades freely.

LTCM hunts for tiny price gaps between similar securities (bonds and other things that trade on markets). It bets those gaps will close, as they usually do. Each win is small.

So the fund borrows. For every dollar of its own money, called its capital, it now holds about 30 dollars of debt. Late in 1997 it handed some capital back to investors but kept its bets just as big.

That raises a question. What are many small, likely wins worth once you count one rare, large loss?

Why does LTCM borrow so heavily: because each trade wins big, or because each trade wins little?

August 1998. John Meriwether, once a top boss at the bond trading firm Salomon Brothers, runs Long-Term Capital Management (LTCM). It's a hedge fund: a private fund for wealthy investors that can make almost any kind of bet.

LTCM hunts for tiny price gaps between two very similar securities (things you can trade, like bonds) and bets that each gap will close. Each win is small. So the fund borrows heavily to make its trades bigger. It now holds about $30 of borrowed money for every $1 of its own.

Most of the time, these trades bring in small, likely gains. The question is what that pile of small wins is worth once you also count a rare, large loss.

If you ran LTCM, which would worry you more: how often a trade loses, or how big the loss is when it does?

August 1998. A fund called Long-Term Capital Management (LTCM) has been running since February 1994. Its founder is John Meriwether, a former vice chairman of the bond firm Salomon Brothers. LTCM is a hedge fund, a private pool of investors' money that trades in many markets.

Its method sounds calm. It finds two similar securities, things like bonds that people buy and sell. Their prices have drifted slightly apart, and LTCM bets the gap will close. Each trade earns only a little, so the fund borrows heavily. It now holds about 30 dollars of debt for every dollar of its own money.

Most trades should win a little. Rarely, one could lose a lot.

If a bet wins most of the time, does that make it a good bet?

That 4% to 5% savings rate is a made-up example, so no real bank changed it. Real banks do change savings rates, though. One big reason is the central bank, a country's top bank, which sets the rate banks pay to borrow from each other overnight. When that rate rises, banks often pay savers more. In our story, that central bank is the US Federal Reserve. On 3 February 1994 its rate stands at 3%, and its committee is about to decide whether to move it.

Because interest starts earning interest too. That's called compounding. Put ₹1,00,000 in at 10% a year. After one year you have ₹1,10,000, so you earned ₹10,000. In year two, the 10% applies to ₹1,10,000, not just your first ₹1,00,000. You end with ₹1,21,000, so year two earned ₹11,000. Each year the pile is bigger, so the same rate adds more money. We'll come back to this in a later Topic. For now we're sticking with how rate moves are described.

CAGR stands for compound annual growth rate. It's the one steady yearly rate that takes money from where it started to where it ended. It counts interest earning interest along the way. Take the example from before: ₹1,00,000 grew to ₹1,21,000 in two years. The CAGR is 10%. That means growing 10% every year gets you exactly there. People use it to sum up growth over many years in one simple number.

Short answer: in our example, no bank did. The 4% to 5% savings rate is made up so the numbers are easy to work with. Real banks change savings rates for a few reasons. The central bank may have moved its own rate. The bank may want more deposits to lend out. Or rival banks may be paying more. Yes, it's the same chain, just from the other side. On savings, the bank pays you interest. On a credit card, you pay interest on what you owe. When the central bank raises its rate, card rates often rise too. A card rate going from 36% to 38% is still 2 points, or 200 basis points, measured exactly the same way.

February 3, 1994, Washington. The Federal Reserve, America's central bank, steers one key rate: the federal funds rate, the interest banks charge each other on overnight loans. Today it stands at 3%. Many investors have borrowed cheaply to buy long-term bonds. Any move in that rate will reach them quickly.

Now your question. Basis points let them name tiny moves in whole numbers.

If the Fed nudges its 3% rate, who would most likely describe the move in basis points: a bond trader or a headline writer?

If the Fed nudged the rate by just a few basis points, would that be less than a full percentage point, or more?
